entries.effect: BOTH ACCESSORS ARE EXPORTED and the getter answers BOOL, because the SDK declares this a readwrite property and not a method: UIViewPropertyAnimator.h:49 reads `@property(nonatomic) BOOL flushUpdates`, so an application that writes `animator.flushUpdates = YES` sends setFlushUpdates: and one that reads it sends flushUpdates. What the pair holds is the honest nothing: the 16.4 SDK's UIViewPropertyAnimator declares no flush and no updateEverything, so there is nothing to forward to, the getter returns NO until a setter stores otherwise, and a 6.1.3 animator runs its animations without the 26.0 flush-on-every-context-change

entries.reason: measured absent, where the row sat `owed` - and owed is not a landing state, the queue's own rulebook says so. THE OWNER IS NOT A CLASS IN ANY RELEASE: UITextInput is a @protocol in 6.1.3, 12.0, 16.0 and 18.0, all four answering `protocol` and not `class` for it, so A CATEGORY CANNOT BE ON A PROTOCOL and there is no port class for this member to live on. THE SELECTOR IS OLD AND THAT IS A TRAP, NOT A REASON: first-rung answers 8.0 for unobscuredContentRect, and in every release that carries it the owner is WebKit's WAKScrollView or WKContentView - 12.0, 16.0 and 18.0 all list the pair, and 6.1.3 lists neither because WKWebView is 8.0 - while UITextInput itself carries the member in no held release. A selector's rung is not its owner's. WHAT THE OLD REASON SAID IS STILL TRUE AND NO LONGER DECIDES: the SDK 26.2 surface does not declare the name, because a 26.4 name cannot appear in a 26.2 surface by construction, so the property's type was never readable here - which is why the accessor this object once carried was a guess with a symbol on it, and why the port writes none. What closes this row is a surface that declares it, read against the same inventories

entries.reason: not carried on NSObject, and this row was naming the wrong class: the 26.2 UIKit surface has this API as -[UIResponder providerForDeferredMenuElement:], introduced 26.0, and no Apple SDK declares it on NSObject. The port answers it exactly where the SDK does - in @implementation UIResponder (CharonUIKit26) at UIKit26_0.m:829 - and that is the row ios26.json carries as -[UIResponder providerForDeferredMenuElement:], with its own reason. NSObject does not get it by inheritance either: UIResponder's superclass is NSObject, not the other way round, so a category on UIResponder adds nothing to NSObject. Measured, not assumed: otool -ov over the object built from UIKit26_0.m at armv7-apple-ios6.1.3 lists -[UIResponder providerForDeferredMenuElement:] under UIResponder and lists nothing at all under NSObject, whose own categories in the same file are CharonUIKit26_EditActions, _MenuBuilder, _SearchBarDelegate, _SplitViewDelegate, _TextFieldDelegate, _TextViewDelegate and _WindowSceneDelegate. An application never writes this spelling - the name it writes is the UIResponder one
entries.effect: nothing answers -providerForDeferredMenuElement: on NSObject, so respondsToSelector: on a plain object answers NO. The name an application writes is -[UIResponder providerForDeferredMenuElement:], which is exported and answers nil, and its row says so
entries.source: the API is declared as a member of UIResponder in the 26.2 UIKit surface, which coordination/corpus/sdk-26.2-surface.tsv records at line 142385 as -[UIResponder providerForDeferredMenuElement:], framework UIKit, kind method, introduced 26.0, via own, with no entry for an NSObject spelling; it is absent from the iPhoneOS16.4 SDK the build compiles against. What NSObject does is measured on the armv7-apple-ios6.1.3 object built from packages/a/apple-backports/UIKit/UIKit26_0.m and read with otool -ov from __objc_classlist and __charon_catlist
